title: A 23-Year-Old Dropout's AI Assistant Is Taking On Zuckerberg's Meta
excerpt: Instinct, built by Noah Shinn, is reportedly raising $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation — weeks after Meta launched its rival, Muse.
body:
• Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that works through texts and phone calls, is in talks to raise $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation, per The Information.
  • The raise would come weeks after a $250 million Series B at $2.25 billion — a near-quadrupling in a month for a company launched in February.
  • Meta launched its competing assistant Muse weeks after Instinct went viral; CEO Mark Zuckerberg says Meta held Muse back over safety concerns.

Noah Shinn was publishing influential AI research as a Northeastern undergraduate before dropping out in 2023. Now 23, the former Sierra researcher has built Instinct, an invite-only personal AI assistant that lives in iMessage and WhatsApp rather than a standalone app. Users text it like a human assistant and hand off practical tasks — travel planning, subscription cancellations, bill negotiation, appointment booking — to an AI agent that operates a phone and computer much as a person would.

The startup

A newer Concierge tier handles tasks that still require actual phone calls, such as booking restaurants that don't take online reservations or getting onto a dentist's cancellation list. The product went viral among Silicon Valley insiders this summer, and Shinn has become one of AI's hottest young founders — now in direct competition with another company started by a college dropout: Meta.

The money

According to The Information, Instinct is in talks to raise $1 billion at a roughly $10 billion valuation, with Sequoia Capital and Benchmark in discussions to lead. The round would land less than a month after a $250 million Series B co-led by Index Ventures and Benchmark at a $2.25 billion pre-money valuation, bringing total funding to $350 million. From a $50 million seed valuation to $10 billion in under five months — for a company launched in February — the trajectory is extreme even by AI-boom standards.

Investor Turner Novak noted that venture capitalists are already promising to get in at $50 billion after missing the early rounds. The catch, skeptics note: Instinct is free, has more than 100,000 users, sometimes lags under heavy demand — and has no proven revenue yet.

The Meta rivalry

Instinct's biggest problem is now Mark Zuckerberg. The Meta CEO pledged to build "personal superintelligence" last year — a project known internally as Hatch — and Meta launched its own AI agent, Muse, weeks after Instinct's breakout. Muse quickly rose to the top of the app store. In a Threads post, Zuckerberg said Meta had been holding Muse back over AI safety and security concerns, as well as practical ones like making sure it followed instructions and didn't buy products without permission.

Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang has mockingly dubbed Shinn's startup "Insect" and posted that Muse is faster — and "hotter." Shinn answered with a smiley face.

"This is the first AI assistant I've recommended my wife and kids, who aren't techies, should use."

— John Borthwick, CEO, Betaworks

Why it's resonating

Early users describe something other chatbots never delivered: an assistant that completes tasks rather than just answering questions. Command Education CEO Christopher Rim, who says he never hired a human assistant, described giving Instinct a Middle East trip itinerary and having it unsolicitedly arrange an airport car service — a free Emirates first-class perk he didn't know he had. The invite-only scarcity adds to the allure.

The diaspora angle

The race is thick with Indian-origin talent on both sides — from the researchers building agentic AI to the Sequoia and Benchmark partners writing the checks. For the diaspora's large tech workforce, the shift from chatbots to assistants that act is also a career signal: the most valuable AI work is moving from models to systems that reliably get things done in the world.

What's next

Whether Instinct can convert hype into a business before Meta's distribution and computing advantages grind it down is the open question. Watch the terms of the $1 billion round — and whether revenue appears before the next one.
